images.filename: Former Railway Line, Tide Mills - geograph.org.uk - 592511.jpg
images.caption: Former Railway Line, Tide Mills Laid in the 1880s to transport shingle from the beach to the help with the construction of the western breakwater just out of picture near the cliffs to the left. After that it was briefly used to collect blue boulders used in pottery glazes. The embedded line is now a footpath that runs from Newhaven to Seaford. The ruins are those of the former Chailey Marine Hospital, the hospital building on the left and the nurses home to the right.

images.filename: Remains of Chailey Marine Hospital - geograph.org.uk - 592496.jpg
images.caption: Remains of Chailey Marine Hospital Built in 1924 as an extension of Chailey Heritage Hospital founded originally to provide for disabled and other handicapped children. The idea was to build a small hospital on the seafront as it was believed sea air was healthy. The foundations to the right were for the actual hospital whilst those further on the left were for the nurses home. Whilst the foundations were concrete the buildings were wooden. The hospital was evacuated and demolished with the rest of Tide Mills in 1940. The embankment on the extreme left was built to hold the waters of the mill pond in whilst Seaford lies straight ahead.

images.caption:
Tide Mills Village Viewed from the site of the former mill. Whilst the mill may have been demolished in 1900 the village that grew up around it continued to operate. The ruins beyond the creek were turned into horse stables during the 1920s in order to rehabilitate race horses by getting them to run in the sea at low tides. A number of the cottages continued to be inhabitated until 1934 when the lack of sanitation and other utilities enabled the local council to condemn them. The last inhabitants were forcibly evicted in 1940 and the buildings destroyed so that the British Army could have a clear field of fire should the Wehrmacht choose Seaford Bay as a landing point.
Beyond the ruins to the left the concrete boards of the former Bishopstone Beach station can be made out whilst in the background is the modern suburb of Bishopstone built on Rookery Hill.

images.caption: Southern End of Mill Drove Now blocked to traffic at the level crossing this is now the far end of Tidemills village street though originally it would have continued eastwards towards the Chailey Marine Hospital. The rails once served a small line that collected shingle and was linked to the mainline near Newhaven Marine Station whilst the pond in the background is the remnants of the former millpond that powered the tide mill.

images.caption:
Bateman's was built around 1634. Rudyard Kipling bought Bateman's in 1902. He and his American wife, Carrie, had discovered the house two years earlier but had been too slow in deciding to buy it and it was let before they could close the deal. When the house came on the market again in 1902, they had no hesitation and bought it along with the surrounding buildings, the mill and 33 acres for £9,300. It had no bathroom, no running water upstairs and no electricity but Kipling loved it. Rudyard Kipling died in 1936 and Carrie continued to live at Bateman's until her death in 1939.

I won a wineglass on eBay to replace one that was broken. The seller lives just off my route to visit my mother. Near his house I saw a sign to Bateman's. It was closed. I must go back whan it is open...
